translations.4473154920495675657: The order in which files leave when a size limit is exceeded. The strategy changes nothing while the cache fits in its limits.
translations.2879339180878659770: Every download moves the file to the front of one queue; when room is needed, the file at the back goes. Simple and predictable. A 60 GiB file downloaded once three days ago outlives a 2 MiB file downloaded fifty times four days ago, and someone trying a model once pushes useful files out.
translations.1914764339029037233: Like LRU, but how long a file has been idle is weighed against how long it takes to fetch again. A 30 GiB shard that took twenty minutes to arrive may stay idle longer than a config.json that comes back in a second. The cost is the measured duration of the file's last fetch from the Hub; files cached before this version are priced from their size with the estimates below.
translations.3416764453398626960: score = weight × ln(cost) − ln(idle time); the lowest score goes first
translations.6608831776456866950: GreedyDual-Size-Frequency, the policy of Squid and of CDN caches. A file is worth frequency × cost ÷ size: a small file that is often downloaded is worth a lot per byte, a large shard downloaded once is worth little. Best hit rate counted in files, but large shards are sacrificed first; avoid it when those are exactly what costs bandwidth. Frequency fades with the half-life.
translations.739862626243855246: Every download adds one to the file's counter, and the counter halves at every half-life. The lowest counter goes first. The HEAD requests clients send to check a file do not count. Size and cost are ignored, and a file that was popular last month stays until the half-life has worn its counter down.
translations.3961640930617584275: A ring: files leave in the order they came in, whether they were read again or not, so the cache turns over at a steady pace and nothing sticks. Suited to an evaluation or CI buffer where each model serves a few days and never again; a file read every day is still fetched again at every turn.
translations.202031623784008083: Cost weight {$START_TAG_SPAN}(0.1 to 2){$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}{$TAG_INPUT}{$START_TAG_SPAN_1}At 1, a file twice as slow to fetch may stay idle twice as long. 0.1 is close to LRU.{$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}
translations.2532740056393865965: Files in the ring {$START_TAG_SPAN}(0 = no limit){$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}{$TAG_INPUT}{$START_TAG_SPAN_1}The first bound reached applies.{$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}
translations.4817484982654175922: Frequency half-life {$START_TAG_SPAN}(hours){$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}{$TAG_INPUT}{$START_TAG_SPAN_1}A download counts half as much after this time. 168 is one week.{$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}
translations.6353022967635050853: Estimated Hub bandwidth {$START_TAG_SPAN}(bytes per second){$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}{$TAG_INPUT}{$START_TAG_SPAN_1}Prices the files whose fetch was not timed.{$CLOSE_TAG_SPAN}
translations.5014659311863682625: Whether a file is stored at all the first time a client asks for it. Many models are tried once and never loaded again; storing them evicts files that are still in use. A file that is not stored is still served, streamed from the Hub. Preloads and files under the minimum size are always stored.
translations.4832142497724927871: Right when most files that are fetched once are fetched again, or when the cache is far larger than what users touch: nothing is ever fetched twice. Wrong for a shared proxy where people try models: each trial pushes files that are still in use out of a full cache.
translations.6781667800678047235: Right for a shared proxy where many models are tried once: a model loaded by one person for one evaluation never takes room. The price is one extra fetch from the Hub for every file that does get used again, and the second user waits for it. The window says how long the first request is remembered.
translations.6702151311833083238: Right when the cache is full and its contents are valuable: a newcomer must earn its place against the file it would push out, counted on recent requests. While the cache has room, everything is stored. Without a total size limit it behaves like storing every file.
